newsitem.title: UK: Britain's new banks to boost total of shareholders.
newsitem.headline: Britain's new banks to boost total of shareholders.

text.p: British building societies may this summer achieve what 18 years of Conservative government has strived for -- a nation of shareholders.

Over the next few months a whole host of building societies -- Britain's mutual mortgage lenders -- will convert into banks, handing out shares to millions of their members in the process and giving the Thatcherite dream of popular capitalism a huge boost.
It could also give some substance to the opposition Labour Party's goal to create a "stakeholding" society.
Labour, streets ahead in the opinion polls, is widely expected to form the next government after May 1 elections.
The Alliance & Leicester launched its shares on the London Stock Exchange on Monday. The price zoomed higher to 570 pence, compared with a maximum anticipated float price of 510p.
About 22 billion pounds ($36 billion) worth of shares in total will be given away by the building societies.

The Halifax alone will give about nine million people shares, the Alliance & Leicester has about 2.4 million members and that still leaves the Woolwich, Northern Rock, the Bristol & West and insurance group Norwich Union.
Proshare, an organisation set up to promote wider share ownership, said the number of British shareholders could double.

There are currently 9.5 million shareholders in Britain, up from three million in 1979. "But after all these conversions, we estimate there will be around 18 or 19 million," a ProShare spokeswoman said.

One of the pillars of Conservative policy in the 1980s and 1990s was the wholesale sell-off of state assets. British Telecom, British Airways, British Gas, British Petroleum and a string of water and electricity utilities were all privatised.
The Conservatives said they would operate more efficiently and profitably in the private sector, a claim that has been borne out in many cases.

The other aim of denationalising state industries -- selling the family silver as critics called it -- was to launch a wave of popular capitalism. That was ex-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's dream.
But while millions more people became shareholders, they only got their hands on a tiny proportion of the stock on offer.

While the Thatcher era saw the number of people holding shares rise from three million to a peak of 11 million in 1989, the vast majority of equity in privatised companies ended up with the large financial institutions -- pensions, insurance funds and the like.

About 27 percent of the Alliance & Leicester's new shareholders have chosen to sell their shares immediately and presumably a lot more will over time. The major institutions will not be slow to gobble those up.
History shows shares from past privatisations have largely ended up in the hands of those big players.

"What tends to happen is you get a high level of initial sales which then slows down," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse Tilney. "You would expect to see something like 80 percent of the shares held by major institutions two years on."
"And the remaining 20 percent will be held in a very large number of hands. We've certainly seen that in the past."

That pattern may not be repeated with building societies, but Jeffrey said that if the 25 to 30 percent of shares sold immediately in Alliance & Leicester was repeated for all the flotations, about double that amount of shares will have been sold by ordinary investors over the following six months.
So the drive to popular capitalism may get a second wind this summer. But it will be pretty thinly spread -- a nation of shareholders with just a handful of shares each. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
